title: AI doesn’t mean you can make bigger games
author: AzibiZubiGames
selftext:
This summer I fell in the trap of AI, where I thought I was able to make any game I wanted with it, by creating little pieces and connecting them, making lots of features and so on.

Yet, as I went on with development, I realised I forgot my original plan and lost myself into adding more and more stuff.

Well, I think the best ideas come when you limit your creativity, and AI doesn’t help with that.

As for now, I will keep making small games by myself, instead of using AI, but in the future, I will surely use this rule of thumb:

Always push for ideas that you can make with your current resources, in a “short” amount of time. If it takes 1 year to make a game without AI, then you must use AI to make it in 6 months, instead of using that full year go make a bigger game.

It’s very counterintuitive to say that you will have double the features if you use AI. Instead, you will have a more uninspired, unoriginal game.

For example: you want to make a story based game, but your dream is too have voice acted cutscenes. Do you have the resources to do so, even without AI? If not, don’t go that route.

Always force yourself to limit your ideas on something real. Also, on code, you might get to a point of having too many lines of code, and you wouldn’t even know how to navigate those, instead of wasting time asking the AI.

comments.body:

comments.author: sevenoutdb
comments.body:
I think this is a fair point to make, but it really depends. What are we making games for? If we are making games as a commercial enterprise, well, you need to make a competitive product, full stop. If it takes you years, then it takes you years. It doesn't take that long to make some short vertical slice of a game, create some kind of reusable/variable hook (a la roguelike/roguelite) and call it done and ship it, but don't be surprised if no one cares.

The games need to have an interesting hook, need to be made with the player in mind, and need to look valuable enough for a player to invest their time into. The time and money invested can maybe, just maybe, be monetized into something profitable.

Scope matters, yes, of course it does, if you can't finish a game and keep adding scope, you will never finish it, and you will never have any indication from real players what works and what doesn't, so if you are adding a bunch of features that you are guessing the player wants, you'd better have a plan to get in front of the kind of player you are making this for and see what they think, and if they think the game is too thin, they will pass, if they think game is too complex, they may also pass. It's a careful balance and thus, I think it's laudable to try to get people to think about limited scope projects that you can get to market and gather information, but that being said, if you know that your game isn't competitive, there is no reason to rush it out, it's like planning your own funeral while you are still alive and well.

replies.author: AzibiZubiGames
replies.body:
The point is that AI might lead you to think that you are good enough to pursue something that you cannot do conceptually.

Like, I can make an rpg with countless systems of power ups, yet I can’t think a way to balance those system together. Probably AI will be able to do so one day, but how can you be sure it will be fun?

Complex games needs abstraction as a tool, which is deeply human (currently). AI won’t increase your capacity to make a fun game.

replies.author: sevenoutdb
replies.body:
I spend the most time actually playing the game, capturing video - discussing it with the co-creator and then writing up feedback and ideas, writing bugs.

I do also create vector art (in the Inkscape app) and do audio editing / composition, and I write dialog, game copy. Feels like I’m creating something.

comments.author: Creepy-Doughnut-5054
comments.body: Thats called scope creeping. This is something you need to refuse right at the begining and make boundries.

replies.author: AzibiZubiGames
replies.body: Yes, and AI is doing the opposite to beginners.

comments.author: PositiveScarcity8909
comments.body: I have the opposite problem, I get too fixated on things not being good enough, even small things and using AI just makes me want to spend so much time fixing small things that don't feel good.

comments.author: LAGameStudio
comments.body: The more game you make, the slower AI becomes even with better models.  It starts writing tests and things accumulate, complexity increases and fwoom, it starts adding features you didn't even ask for.  It's not all a walk in the park when you say "Make me X and Y" .. so many times I justed it to move a button from A to B and it ended up doing something entirely unintended.

comments.author: InformationTop5376
comments.body:
I’ve never actually thought about bolting on every feature I can think of. Sure I’ve got lots of ideas for my game but that doesn’t mean they should go in. I use AI heavily to help me research where certain game mechanics have been successful in different games and then what were the failure modes and traps, so I can be sure to avoid them in my game.

I think part of my approach is that I’m also a dev at my day job (non games industry), so I understand scope creep from first hand experience. And what it can do to a project.

comments.author: ZymzAlchemy
comments.body:
Properly roadmapped, blueprinted and constructed properly the scope is irrelevant.  
AI is a tool. The rest is on you, the creator/developer/designer/architect.  
Be well and keep creating.
